title: Building (systems) software with Nix
excerpt: Something I found incredibly frustrating when I started programming was that I could not spend more time building projects and instead had to fight with erro...
content_html:
Something I found incredibly frustrating when I started programming was that I could not spend more time building projects and instead had to fight with errors that seemed like a distraction. These major time sinks didn’t seem more than an inconvenience that were preventing me from making progress and focus on the fun stuff.

Even worse, pretty often what used to work would stop to and it would not be clear why. At the time, I didn’t have the knowledge to even hypothesise what might have happened.

Years later, and despite having levelled up as an engineer, I suppose I tend to feel something similar, especially when working on systems software. The project that built or run yesterday is no longer doing so in the same way. Nowadays I can come up with some possible reasons for this, test some theories, and so on, which is neat, but often this is a big time invesment, and more importantly, it’s work that I don’t find too enjoyable and that takes time from what I want to do: actually building software. The fun stuff.

There you have it, another moving target

Most modern programming languages come with package managers (bundler, cargo, npm, etc) that help fetch dependencies, and among other things they do their best to ensure that they aren’t altered without the user knowing. This is essential for security, and also helps to keep consistency across machines. This is a big improvement from how most people were building software not that long ago.

This is not bullet-proof, though, since there are other sources of variability. The compiler or interpreter version, system-provided libraries, environment variables, etc.

If this weren’t enough, when dealing with systems-level software, we might be using native libraries, and exercise the operating system in ways most other software might never do! The more surface area, the higher the chances of the software we depend changing their behaviour over time.

What about our operating system kernel? From an abstract perspective, it’s another library that code interfaces with. This leads us to some of the fastest evolving parts in the Linux kernel: the BPF subsystem, the fancy new sched_ext schedulers, or io_uring, among others.

When it comes to the whole operating system, a seemingly scheduled routine system update can update part of the toolchain such as the compiler or the linker. A system library that your code uses might change, or even the kernel itself! This can prevent your code from not building, or even worse: changing its behaviour.

One of each, please

I haven’t checked the data but I would find surprising if the BPF ecosystem is not one of the most fast evolving ones in Linux. This is great, because it means that every kernel release comes with exciting new features and fixes, but it can add spiciness to our development (and production!) environments. Besides that, for a basic libbpf based application written in Rust, we depend on:

  • Rust compiler (rustc) and related tools (cargo);
  • C compiler(s) (clang). Typically BPF code gets compiled with clang, but most Linux systems use gcc for other native code;
  • Native dependencies (libelf, zlib, libbpf, libc);
  • Rust dependencies;
  • Linux kernel headers (vmlinux.h), and, if generated at build time, the system’s BTF information and bpftool to produce the header file;
  • Kernel-side of BPF tooling (system call layer, verifier, etc);
  • Static linker(s);
  • Dynamic loader (ld.so);
  • The environment (env);

If I were to bet on this list being complete, I would probably lose. But hopefully it’s enough to illustrate the problem we are dealing with.

We are a single apt/dnf/$YOUR_PACKAGE_MANAGER away from large parts of our software dependencies potentially changing. By default, it’s just one part of the equation that’s fully understandable and under our control: the Rust dependencies (assuming there’s a Cargo.lock in SCM). Perhaps also libbpf, since it’s vendored by default.

If you are unlucky, the burden of hunting for differences is on you. More often that not, figuring out what the previous state of the system was is a herculean task.

Taming the dependency chaos

One of the core ideas behind modern dependency managers is the inclusion of lockfiles. They represent a serialised view of the dependencies that were “locked in” at some point. Among other data, this includes the package location, its precise version, and a checksum to ensure it’s not tampered with or corrupt.

Wouldn’t it be neat if we could apply it for all the items in the list above? Turns out there are more than one implementation of this idea, one them being Nix. Nix is:

  • a package manager (provides libraries, binaries, etc);
  • a build system (instructions on how to build code);
  • a programming language used in the above;
  • a Linux distribution, NixOS, based on the eponymous package manager and build system;
  • a bunch of infrastructure such as a build farm, cache, etc to support the above;

Here we are referring to the package manager and build system bits, which work in most Linux distributions and other operating systems such as MacOS. In fact, while I have been using these for almost 2 years now, I am a new NixOS user. There is a lot of great content online by folks that know way more about Nix than I do on the language, developer environments, how Nix works under the hood, etc;

For a simplified mental model, the pieces that are useful to know are that the “official” Nix packages are in this repo called nixpkgs, and that if we want to have something like a Cargo.lock for Nix, we probably want to use flakes. By using flakes we can select a particular revision of the nixpkgs repository and every dependency we use will match what’s defined and built in it.

A Rust + BPF environment using Nix

See runqslower, with a Nix flake similar to the one that I use. I commented it enough to make it more understandable to newcomers, but tried not to be too verbose.

Once Nix in installed, a simple nix develop brings an environment with all the required software. The best part is that it’s of course reproducible. If it builds and runs now, it will run and build tomorrow. And if it that’s not the case, we know that it’s due to some other environmental change that’s outside of the control of Nix and Cargo.

Real examples

This is all good, but nothing better than concrete examples on how this setup has helped me so far:

No more “works in my machine”

Contributors to the projects that use Nix, despite running different ditrubutions or operating systems have a consistent developer environment that very rarely breaks

Bisecting changes becomes easier

Since the package manager and build system are closely related, bisecting for changes can be a bit easier than what you might be used to. As a real example, the BPF code of one of my projects loaded fine in my kernel if compiled with clang 19 but wasn’t accepted if clang 21 was in use.

The code to select a different clang/LLVM version wasn’t more than 10 lines of code, and after not too long it was clear that it was the ISA v3 for BPF becoming a default which tripped some older kernels/

Better defaults

One of the projects I use that’s written in C++ crashed in production but only under Nix. This is due to a more strict security policy than other software packagers and the usage of -DD_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 by default. The undefined behaviour that would have been incredibly tricky to spot, and maybe even caused data corruption, was a clear crash thanks to this flag. This issue was shared upstream and the fix was rolled out some months ago.

Dependency customisation, without the pain

No need to patch build systems that I might not be familiar with. Additionally Nix derivations, similar to rules if you come from buck2/bazel compose well.

Faster builds

Thanks to being a proper build system, only what’s necessary to be rebuilt is rebuilt. If you are unfamiliar with this concept, think of your favourite spreadsheet software with cells referencing other cells. Only data that needs to be recomputed will be refreshed.

The other source of speed comes from the smart caching that Nix, and other build systems can do thanks to being reproducible. The clang/LLVM bisect didn’t rebuild millions of lines of code since there were many cache hits.

What about the kernel itself?

This write-up is getting a bit long, but that’s something I can maybe talk about in a future post if there’s interest.

Conclusion

This setup has helped me focus on the parts that bring me the most joy and has mostly stayed out of my way, which is exactly what you I want in my build systems and package managers.

The Nix ecosystem and tooling is vast and I only know a small fraction of it but I am looking forward to continue using it and learning NixOS.

Note: No AI was used in this writing.

content_html_zh:
当我开始编程时，我发现非常令人沮丧的是，我无法花更多时间构建项目，而不得不与看似分散注意力的错误作斗争。 这些主要的时间消耗似乎只是一种不便，阻碍了我取得进步并专注于有趣的事情。

更糟糕的是，过去有效的方法常常会失效，而且原因也不清楚。 当时，我什至没有知识来假设可能会发生什么。

几年后，尽管我已经晋升为工程师，但我想我还是有类似的感觉，尤其是在从事系统软件工作时。 昨天构建或运行的项目不再以同样的方式运行。 如今，我可以为此提出一些可能的原因，测试一些理论，等等，这很简洁，但通常这是一项很大的时间投资，更重要的是，我觉得这项工作不太有趣，而且需要时间来完成我想做的事情：实际构建软件。 有趣的东西。

就是这样，另一个移动目标

大多数现代编程语言都带有包管理器（bundler、cargo、npm 等）来帮助获取依赖项，并且它们会尽力确保它们不会在用户不知情的情况下被更改。 这对于安全性至关重要，并且还有助于保持机器之间的一致性。 与不久前大多数人构建软件的方式相比，这是一个很大的进步。

但这并不是万无一失的，因为还有其他可变性来源。 编译器或解释器版本、系统提供的库、环境变量等。

如果这还不够，在处理系统级软件时，我们可能会使用本机库，并以大多数其他软件可能永远不会做的方式运行操作系统！ 表面积越大，我们所依赖的软件随着时间的推移改变其行为的机会就越大。

我们的操作系统内核呢？ 从抽象的角度来看，它是另一个与代码交互的库。 这让我们了解了 Linux 内核中发展最快的一些部分：BPF 子系统、奇特的新 sched_ext 调度程序或 io_uring 等。

当涉及到整个操作系统时，看似预定的例行系统更新可以更新部分工具链，例如编译器或链接器。 您的代码使用的系统库可能会发生变化，甚至内核本身也可能会发生变化！ 这可以防止您的代码无法构建，甚至更糟：改变其行为。

请每人一份

我还没有检查过数据，但如果 BPF 生态系统不是 Linux 中发展最快的生态系统之一，我会感到惊讶。 这很棒，因为这意味着每个内核版本都带有令人兴奋的新功能和修复，但它可以为我们的开发（和生产！） 环境。 除此之外，对于用 Rust 编写的基于 libbpf 的基本应用程序，我们依赖于：

  • Rust编译器（rustc）和相关工具（cargo）；
  • C 编译器 (clang)。 通常，BPF 代码是使用 clang 编译的，但大多数 Linux 系统使用 gcc 来编译其他本机代码；
  • 本机依赖项（libelf、zlib、libbpf、libc）；
  • Rust 依赖项；
  • Linux 内核头文件 (vmlinux.h)，如果在构建时生成，则还包括系统的 BTF 信息和用于生成头文件的 bpftool；
  • BPF工具的内核端（系统调用层、验证器等）；
  • 静态链接器；
  • 动态加载器（ld.so）；
  • 环境（env）；

如果我打赌这份清单是完整的，我可能会输。 但希望这足以说明我们正在处理的问题。

我们只有一个 apt/dnf/$YOUR_PACKAGE_MANAGER，远离可能发生变化的大部分软件依赖项。 默认情况下，它只是等式中完全可以理解且在我们控制之下的一部分：Rust 依赖项（假设 SCM 中有 Cargo.lock）。 也许还有 libbpf，因为它是默认提供的。

如果你运气不好，寻找差异的重担就落在你身上了。 更常见的是，弄清楚系统之前的状态是一项艰巨的任务。

驯服依赖混乱

现代依赖管理器背后的核心思想之一是包含锁定文件。 它们代表了在某个时刻“锁定”的依赖关系的序列化视图。 除其他数据外，这包括包位置、其精确版本以及确保其不被篡改或损坏的校验和。

如果我们可以将它应用于上面列表中的所有项目，那不是很整洁吗？ 事实证明，这个想法有不止一种实现方式，其中之一就是 Nix。 尼克斯是：

  • 包管理器（提供库、二进制文件等）；
  • 构建系统（有关如何构建代码的说明）；
  • 上述中使用的编程语言；
  • Linux 发行版 NixOS，基于同名的包管理器和构建系统；
  • 一堆基础设施，例如构建场、缓存等来支持上述内容；

这里我们指的是包管理器和构建系统位，它们适用于大多数 Linux 发行版和其他操作系统（例如 MacOS）。 事实上，虽然我已经使用它们近两年了，但我是 NixOS 的新用户。 网上有很多关于 Nix 的精彩内容，他们比我更了解 Nix，包括语言、开发环境、Nix 的工作原理等；

对于简化的心理模型，需要了解的有用信息是“官方”Nix 软件包位于名为 nixpkgs 的存储库中，并且如果我们想要为 Nix 提供类似 Cargo.lock 之类的东西，我们可能需要使用 flake。 通过使用 flakes，我们可以选择 nixpkgs 存储库的特定版本，并且我们使用的每个依赖项都将与其中定义和构建的内容相匹配。

使用 Nix 的 Rust + BPF 环境

请参阅 runqslower，它具有与我使用的类似的 Nix 薄片。 我对其进行了足够的注释，以使新人更容易理解，但尽量不要太冗长。

一旦安装了 Nix，一个简单的 nix 开发就会带来一个包含所有必需软件的环境。 最好的部分是它当然是可复制的。 如果它现在构建并运行，那么它明天也会运行和构建。 如果情况并非如此，我们知道这是由于 Nix 和 Cargo 无法控制的其他一些环境变化造成的。

真实例子

这一切都很好，但没有什么比具体的例子更好地说明这个设置到目前为止如何帮助我了：

不再“在我的机器上工作”

使用 Nix 的项目的贡献者，尽管运行不同的版本或操作系统，但仍具有一致的开发环境，很少出现中断

平分更改变得更容易

由于包管理器和构建系统密切相关，因此对等更改可能比您习惯的更容易一些。 作为一个真实的例子，如果使用 clang 19 编译，我的一个项目的 BPF 代码可以很好地加载到我的内核中，但如果使用 clang 21 则不会被接受。

选择不同 clang/LLVM 版本的代码不超过 10 行代码，不久之后就很明显，BPF 的 ISA v3 成为默认值，导致一些旧内核/

更好的默认值

我使用的一个用 C++ 编写的项目在生产中崩溃了，但仅在 Nix 下崩溃。 这是由于比其他软件打包程序更严格的安全策略以及默认使用 -DD_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2。 未定义的行为本来很难被发现，甚至可能导致数据损坏，但由于这个标志，导致了明显的崩溃。 这个问题已在上游共享，并且修复程序已在几个月前推出。

依赖项定制，无痛

无需修补我可能不熟悉的构建系统。 另外，Nix 的推导，类似于规则，如果你来自 Buck2/bazel 则可以很好地组合。

更快的构建

由于是一个适当的构建系统，只有需要重建的内容才会被重建。 如果您不熟悉这个概念，请想象一下您最喜欢的电子表格软件，其中的单元格引用其他单元格。 只有需要重新计算的数据才会被刷新。

速度的另一个来源来自 Nix 和其他构建系统由于可重复性而可以实现的智能缓存。 clang/LLVM bisect 没有重建数百万行代码，因为有很多缓存命中。
